title: Model Catalog Demo - HorizonAI
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked HorizonAI thru the Model Catalog: selecting open models, interpreting benchmark rows, and reading the compatibility matrix. Discussed hosted vs dedicated cost/latency tradeoffs, private deployment constraints (VPC/KMS), and Optimize recommendations (quantization, batching, cache). Agreed to run a pilot benchmark on HorizonAI ticketing workload and share model-compatibility spreadsheet and pricing by EOD.
next_steps: Ethan to share model-compatibility matrix CSV and benchmark spreadsheet by 2026-11-05
Maya to send pricing and pilot contract template by 2026-11-06
HorizonAI to provide sample ticketing prompt set and traffic profile by 2026-11-08
action_items: Ethan Chen (SE): export and share compatibility matrix + benchmark raw results, due 2026-11-05
Maya Patel (AE): send pilot pricing & contract template, due 2026-11-06
Daniel Price (HorizonAI): upload sample prompt set and 7-day traffic histogram, due 2026-11-08
transcript:
00:00 Maya (AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, with me is Ethan our solutions engineer. Can you all hear us okay?
00:04 Sofia (CTO): Yes, we can, thanks. This is Sofia, thanks for setting this up.
00:07 Daniel (ML Eng): Daniel here, excited to see model catalog and the benchmarking stuff.
00:11 Maya (AE): Great. Quick agenda: we'll demo the model catalog in the console, show how the API surfaces model choices, run through benchmark numbers and the compatibility matrix (GPU / quant / latency), then Ethan will cover Optimize suggestions for cost/latency. We'll leave time for Q&A.
00:26 Ethan (SE): One small callout — we'll show a few open models we've curated, and also how Redwood maps variants to compatible hardware and quant profiles, which I know is important for you given your on-prem ambitions.
00:36 Priya (DevOps): Yup that's the big one for us. We have H100 in some clusters and A100 in others; want to make sure models work across both, and also how KMS keys plug into the private deployment.
00:49 Ethan (SE): Totally. We'll show the compatibility matrix where each model row shows supported backends and tested quantization (8-bit, 4-bit), and we annotate expected token latency for typical seq lengths.
01:02 Maya (AE): Starting in the console — heading to Model Catalog now. You'll see we filter by license (open vs commercial), size, and task (chat/generation/embeddings). For HorizonAI's ticketing use case, we looked at small-to-medium open chat models with good instruction-following.
01:18 Ethan (SE): Here's an example: the "OpenChat-20B" entry — note the benchmark badge: 65 ms median token latency on H100 with 4-bit quant and 3.2k context, throughput ~280 tokens/sec per GPU in continuous batching. Those numbers are from our internal benchmark suite but we include raw CSVs too.
01:40 Daniel (ML Eng): 65 ms per token seems decent — is that end-to-end including network and prefix cache warmup?
01:47 Ethan (SE): Good question. That number is server-side inference only, measured at the runtime in our Dedicated environment. It assumes KV cache warm (i.e., generation after context loaded). If you measure end-to-end via the hosted API you'll add small network RTT — typically 10–40 ms depending on region. We also provide sample curl scripts to replicate the test.
02:06 Sofia (CTO): And what about A100 numbers? We run mainly A100-80GB in our private racks.
02:11 Ethan (SE): Right — for A100 we publish a separate column in the compatibility matrix. For OpenChat-20B we saw ~95 ms median token latency in 4-bit on A100, throughput roughly 210 tokens/sec. There is a note about kernel optimizations: some newer attention kernels run faster on H100.
02:26 Daniel (ML Eng): Are those kernels automatic or do we need to recompile?
02:29 Ethan (SE): Redwood's runtime selects kernels automatically based on model architecture and hardware, but for Private deployments we ship a small profiler job you run once that samples your sequence distributions and pins kernel choices. We wire that into the console as an optional step.
02:45 Maya (AE): Switching to the API tab — you can see how model selection maps to the endpoint. If you specify model=openchat-20b@v1 and region=us-west, Redwood routes to the best compatible instance class, and you can override to force Dedicated or Private if you have a pinned capacity.
03:02 Priya (DevOps): For Private deployments, how does KMS integrate? We need AES-256 and a custom HSM-backed key.
03:09 Ethan (SE): In Private we support customer-managed keys via KMS and HSM. The console shows integration status — we store logs of KMS operations in the audit trail. There is an RBAC role for key admins.
03:22 Sofia (CTO): SOC 2 / ISO documentation? Our security team will ask.
03:25 Maya (AE): We'll send the SOC 2 and ISO artifacts; Ethan will attach the security whitepaper and architecture for VPC/air-gapped installs after the call.
03:33 Ethan (SE): Back to compatibility matrix: you'll notice a column labeled "quantized friendly" — that flags models where we saw <3% drop in instruction-following evals when going from fp16 to 4-bit. For HorizonAI's ticket summarization, we validated on a recall-focused F1 style metric.
03:50 Daniel (ML Eng): Can you share those eval prompts? We want to run them on our dataset.
03:54 Ethan (SE): Yep — we'll share the eval set and the raw CSVs. The console also supports exporting the benchmark harness so you can run it locally; it spits out latency percentiles and generation quality metrics.
04:08 Maya (AE): I want to highlight the "Compatibility Notes" popover — it lists caveats like tokenizers with long byte-level tokens, or models that require specific CUDA toolkit versions. We surfaced a few quirks for small models that break on L4 GPUs.
04:24 Priya (DevOps): We also have GPU-fleet heterogeneity — some nodes are A100, others H100, and a few L4s for non-critical workloads. Does Redwood support routing by GPU type?
04:33 Ethan (SE): Yes — you can define routing policies: prefer lowest-latency (H100), or cost-optimized (L4 for embeddings), or region-first. The model catalog shows which model variants are compatible per GPU. We also support automatic fallbacks to a compatible variant if your preferred instance is busy.
04:50 Daniel (ML Eng): About Optimize: what are the typical wins you see using auto-batching + prefix cache?
04:55 Ethan (SE): On average, we see 20–45% token-cost reduction from KV caching for chat-heavy workloads, and batching can improve GPU utilization up to 3x for bursty traffic. Optimize recommends batching windows based on your latency SLOs — you can tune time-window size in the console.
05:13 Sofia (CTO): Any regressions to output quality from batching? We've seen occasional weirdness with very large batch sizes.
05:18 Ethan (SE): Good callout. We tune per-model batch size limits in the catalog. The Optimize recommendations include per-model max-batch to keep quality within a threshold; the console highlights any models where large batches degraded eval scores.
05:33 Maya (AE): Quick demo of the benchmark CSV export — here's median p50/p90/p99 latencies across GPUs, and a separate sheet for accuracy/regression vs baseline. You can also toggle simulated traffic to see cost estimates in the Optimize tab.
05:50 Daniel (ML Eng): Is there a way to see token-level cost per model variant?
05:54 Maya (AE): Yes there's a cost breakdown in Optimize: cost per input token, cost per output token, and an effective cost per complete response based on average response lengths. That ties into ROI calculators we can share.
06:08 Priya (DevOps): On private deployment, if we pin a capacity (Dedicated), what's the SLA for tail latencies?
06:14 Maya (AE): For Dedicated we offer SLOs — 99th percentile tail latency SLAs are configurable with your contract. We can share example SLA language; typically customers pick a target and then we size the reserved pool accordingly.
06:27 Ethan (SE): Also note for on-prem we provide an operator guide and a sizing worksheet. For your ticketing workload if you send us the 95th percentile request size and qps, we can estimate GPU count and expected tail p99.
06:39 Daniel (ML Eng): We'll share the 7-day histogram as requested.
06:43 Maya (AE): Quick pause for questions — anything else on model selection?
06:46 Sofia (CTO): One question — licensing. If we use an open model that has a non-commercial clause, how do you flag that?
06:52 Ethan (SE): The catalog flags license type prominently; non-commercial or restricted models are excluded from the default recommendations for enterprise accounts. We can add a filter to only show business-usable models.
07:03 Daniel (ML Eng): Regarding tokenizer differences — some of our prompts have lots of emojis and code snippets, do you recommend specific models?
07:10 Ethan (SE): Models with byte-level tokenizers handle emojis and code more predictably. The catalog has a tokenization robustness score based on a synthetic suite. We'll point out the top 3 models for your prompt profile in the export.
07:25 Maya (AE): Wrapping to Optimize: we ran a quick heuristic on your sample — using OpenChat-20B 4-bit on H100 with KV caching and a 30ms batching window reduced cost by ~32% while keeping p95 latency under 400ms in our sim. Caveat: real numbers depend on your live traffic mix.
07:45 Sofia (CTO): Sounds promising. For pilot, we'd like Redwood to run a benchmark against our sample prompts on both H100 private racks and your hosted dedicated pool to compare.
07:54 Maya (AE): That's doable — action items: Ethan to share compatibility CSV and benchmark harness, Maya to send pricing/pilot template, Daniel to upload sample prompts and traffic hist.
08:05 Daniel (ML Eng): Sounds good. One last item — can we get a quick note about fallbacks if we exceed capacity? Our incident response requires deterministic failover behavior.
08:14 Ethan (SE): Redwood supports deterministic fallback policies: route to a cheaper model variant, route to a different region, or queue with a defined max wait. We'll include the policy examples in the follow-up docs.
08:26 Priya (DevOps): Great. Also will you show the audit logs for inference requests? Need that for compliance.
08:31 Maya (AE): Yes audit logs and request-level tracing are in the Console; we can demo that in the pilot kickoff.
08:37 Sofia (CTO): Thank you — this is helpful.
08:40 Maya (AE): Cool. We'll recap next steps and follow-ups in an email. Thanks everyone for your time.
08:45 Ethan (SE): Thanks all.
08:47 Sofia (CTO): Thanks.
08:48 End of meeting.
